blocks.text: The July Crisis and the Responsibility Debate

segments.text: Germany offered strong (“blank cheque”) support to Austria-Hungary; Russia mobilised to support Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and France; and the invasion of neutral Belgium brought Britain into the war — with compressed military mobilisation timetables sharply reducing the room available for diplomacy at each stage. Historians continue to disagree over the relative responsibility of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia, France and other powers; a strong answer distinguishes the long-term systemic tension that made Europe dangerous from the specific July 1914 decisions that turned a regional dispute into a general war.

items.text: The two rival pre-war alliance blocs whose mutual fear of encirclement contributed to the crisis dynamic.
The rapid, compressed sequence of diplomatic and military decisions following Sarajevo that escalated a regional dispute into general war.
Separate long-term causes from the immediate trigger; build a July Crisis sequence showing who made which decision and when.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why was pre-1914 Europe a dangerous international system, and why did leaders fail to contain the Sarajevo crisis?”
Do not use “MAIN” as the entire answer; each factor needs concrete evidence and a July Crisis explanation.
Do not say the assassination alone caused the war; it was the trigger within an already dangerous international system.
Do not imply all alliance obligations automatically forced war; governments made specific political and military choices at each stage.
The Triple Alliance linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy; Britain, France and Russia formed the Triple Entente.
Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1908, angering Serbia and Russia.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914; escalation during the July Crisis turned a regional confrontation into general war.
Structure any origins-of-WWI answer in two explicit parts: why the system was dangerous before 1914, and why leaders failed to contain the July 1914 crisis specifically.
The Bosnian annexation crisis (Topic 4’s Congress of Berlin outcome) and the Balkan Wars are the direct causal bridge from the Eastern Question into 1914.
